You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: AI Industry Chain Weekly Report — TSMC Raises Capital Expenditure, Acceleration of 800V and Liquid Cooling, Photonic Interconnect and PCB Expansion

TEXT:
TL;DR
1. TSMC provided the strongest validation of demand this week: Q2 2026 revenue at $40.2 billion, a 12% increase quarter-on-quarter and 34% year-on-year, with Q3 guidance at $44.6—45.8 billion; 2026 capital expenditure raised to $60—64 billion. Demand has expanded from GPU to CPU, custom chips, and network chips; advanced process technology and packaging remain in short supply, and there are no typical signs of capacity expansion "for inventory's sake" on the manufacturing side.
2. As rack power evolves from tens of kW toward 600kW and eventually 1MW, power delivery, cooling, and data transmission are becoming more decisive for system delivery than individual chips. 800V DC can reduce current, copper usage, and multi-stage conversion losses, while liquid cooling mitigates the heat flow issues of high-density racks; both are not remote concepts but fundamental prerequisites for the next-generation rack deployment.
3. "Less water" does not mean "less electricity". It is expected that by 2035, around 56% of newly added global data center capacity and 55% of U.S. new capacity will be exposed to high temperatures, humidity, or water resource constraints; some nearly waterless heat dissipation solutions may consume about 25%—45% more electricity. Cooling, grid access, on-site power, and community permits must be evaluated as one system.
4. High-speed interconnects are shifting competition from port count to power consumption, density, and packaging. The Ethernet switch market is expected to grow from about $50 billion in 2025 to over $200 billion by 2035, while the cross-data-center interconnect market may rise from around $9 billion in 2025 to about $33 billion in 2030. 800G, 1.6T, co-packaged optics, silicon photonics, fiber arrays, and high-specification optical fibers are forming an integrated upgrade chain.
5. PCBs and copper-clad laminates are not just passive beneficiaries but direct winners from upgrading AI system specifications. Shennan Circuit's Q2 net profit guidance shows a year-on-year increase of 44%—67%, with Wuxi expansions, 1.6T optical module boards, and server/switch boards contributing incrementally; Shengyi Technology's M9/M10, PTFE, and high-layer board routes, Han's Laser's drilling equipment, and IBIDEN's high-end ABF substrates respectively correspond to value improvement in materials, equipment, and packaging substrates.
6. Evidence on the application side is clearly stratified: electronic design automation intelligent agents already show measurable manpower gaps and charging models, while robotics still mainly depend on mass production pace, and AI PCs face the contradiction of higher penetration but fewer total shipments. Not all "AI applications" should be treated as having the same profitability realization speed.
7. The biggest counterevidence is no longer the sudden disappearance of computing demand, but the mismatch between delivery speed and capital return. Local suspensions, disputes over residential electricity and water use, platform delays, fragmented supplier shares, storage and material price hikes, as well as overvaluations can all lead to strong demand translating into lower-than-expected profits or deferred revenue recognition.

Optical Communication, CPO, PCB, and High-Speed Interconnect
Data Center Cooling, Power, and Electricity
5. Remaining chapters
6. Remaining chapters
7. Remaining chapters
AI demand has not cooled off, but investment logic has shifted from “having enough computing power” to “who can deliver power, cooling, interconnection, and mass production on time.”
General Assessment This Week
The most important change this week is that the credibility of AI capital expenditure has risen again, but the order of beneficiaries is being reshuffled. In the past, the market mainly questioned how many GPUs cloud providers would purchase; now the more critical questions are: Can advanced nodes and packaging be expanded? Is there enough rack power? Can the heat be dissipated? Do switching networks and optical interconnects match? Most importantly, can whole cabinets be delivered on time? Any weak link can turn chip orders into inventory waiting for installation; any persistent bottleneck can shift the profit pool from accelerators to power, cooling, interconnects, substrates, and manufacturing equipment.
[...]
Custom chip market share competition will continue, but the arrival of a second supplier need not be equated with the clear market leader's loss of all advantage. MediaTek joining the Google TPU supply chain proves cloud providers seek to reduce single-source risk; Broadcom still holds advantages in HBM integration, advanced packaging, large-scale deployment, and system execution. A more reasonable conclusion is that single-client share may diversify, but the overall custom chip market expands, and new clients partly offset share changes. Next steps should track tapeout, mass production, chip value per gigawatt, and new client deployments—not just the supplier list.
